1:
The reign opens on a boy of eight set upon the throne of Judah, and the witnesses read in that tender age both a marvel and a summons. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks that Josiah's infancy did not debar him from his right, and that he reigned thirty and one years, a considerable time; yet he fears that in the early years, the child being obliged to leave the management to others, things went much as they had in his father Amon's day, so that the reformation could not begin until his twelfth year. Josiah could not, like Hezekiah, fall about it immediately. Henry adds the note that will govern the whole chapter — while yet young, about sixteen, the king began to seek after God, though he had not so good an education as Manasseh had, for 'those that seek him early shall find him.'

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the Chronicler's account beside the older record. It agrees in all essentials with the representation in 2 Kings 22 and 23, but is chronologically more exact and in many parts more complete. Where the book of Kings views the whole reform in its connection with the discovery of the book of the law, the Chronicle keeps the events apart and describes them according to their order in time: as early as the eighth year the youth began to seek the God of his ancestor David, and in the twelfth year to purge Jerusalem and Judah of idolatry. The reformed John Gill is content to fix the bare datum — eight years old at his accession — and to send the reader to the parallel for the rest.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the road the chapter will travel: Josiah reigns thirty-one years and destroys idolatry from Judah northward through Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and even to Naphtali; he repairs the temple and gathers money for it; Hilkiah finds the book of the law, which Shaphan reads before the king; the alarmed king consults Huldah the prophetess; and at the last the people make a covenant with God and serve him all Josiah's days. The other grammatical-historical witness, Charles Ellicott, adds only what the Chronicler omits and Kings preserves — the name of the king's mother, Jedidah the daughter of Adaiah of Boscath, recorded at 2 Kings 22:1. The witnesses do not divide; together they frame a reign that a child's early seeking of God would make the last great light of Judah before the dark.
3:
Two dates govern the verse, and the witnesses attend to both the seeking and the purging they mark. The reformed John Gill fixes the eighth year of the reign as the sixteenth of Josiah's age, though he records that Kimchi placed the seeking in the very year of his accession, when he was but eight, and that Jarchi read the clause 'though he was young, he began to seek after the God of David his father.' To seek God, Gill explains, was to pray unto him, to seek the knowledge of him and the true manner of his worship — his will, his commands, his ordinances; and the Targum renders it finely, to seek instruction and doctrine of the Lord God of David, that he might be taught the ways his great ancestor had walked in.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the significance of the king's youth. It was in the sixteenth year of his age, 'when he was entering into the age of temptation,' and had the administration of his kingdom wholly in his own power, with none to restrain him — 'even then he begins to be religious in good earnest.' The seeking was not the piety of a sheltered child but the deliberate choice of a young man who might have done as he pleased.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that these precise specifications of time are peculiar to the Chronicler, and that the twelfth year was perhaps when Josiah began to govern alone. He cautions against reading the verse too rigidly: it is not said that the whole extirpation of idolatry was completed in the twelfth year — indeed v.33 implies the contrary — but the writer, having begun the story of the destruction of the idolatrous objects, naturally carries it through to its close, though the finishing properly belongs to the eighteenth year, as the comparison of 2 Kings 22:3 with 2 Kings 23:4 shows. He therefore rejects the suspicions of the critics — that the Chronicler put the purging first merely to prove the pious king needed no prompting, or to clear him of the reproach of tolerating the abomination for eighteen years. The 'high places' he ties to 2 Kings 23:5 and following, the 'groves' to the Asherim of 2 Kings 23:4. The witnesses do not divide; Gill and Wesley dwell on the early seeking of a young king, Ellicott on the ordered chronology and the innocence of the historian's arrangement — together framing a reformation that began in the heart before it fell upon the idols.
4:
The demolition begins with the altars of the Baals, and the witnesses mark that the king did not merely command it but oversaw it. The reformed John Gill notes that Josiah 'went in person, and saw it done'; these were the altars Manasseh had reared, which, though cast out at his humiliation, his son Amon had set up again. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms from the parallel at 2 Kings 23:16 that the king personally superintended the work of destruction, and unfolds the several objects: the 'images' were sun-statues, as at 2 Chronicles 14:4, hewn down from above the altars; the 'molten images' were rather the sacred pillars, the maççeboth of 2 Kings 23:14; and the closing clause he renders literally, that Josiah 'sprinkled upon the face of the graves' of those who had sacrificed to the idols the dust he had made of them, as though the very graves were guilty — where the older account at 2 Kings 23:6 relates this only of the temple Asherah.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse together with the next, and explain the strewing of the dust upon the graves and the burning of the priests' bones as one act of defilement: the Chronicler summarizes here what 2 Kings 23:13-14 and 2 Kings 23:16-20 relate at length — the pollution of the high places by the bones of the dead, that the sites might never be used again.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lifts the scene into a maxim on kings and nations. 'How often have these been broken down, and how soon set up again!' The religion of a land, he observes, is as the religion of its king: when the king was idolatrous, up went the altars and the incense rose in ceaseless clouds to vanity; when the king was truly religious, down went the altars and the images were broken; and 'in all these cases the people were as one man with the king.' The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the king's personal zeal and the identity of the shattered objects; Keil sets the strewn dust and the defiled graves in the pattern of a thorough desecration; Clarke draws the sobering political lesson that a nation's worship follows its throne. Between them they show a reformation that was not content to remove the idols but ground them to powder and scattered the powder on the graves of their worshippers, that Judah might be left no relic to return to.
5:
The burning of the priests' bones upon their own altars carries, for the witnesses, both a grim justice and the fulfilment of an ancient word. The reformed John Gill reads the act as done 'in detestation of their idolatry, and to deter from it,' and hears in it the ringing of a prophecy uttered 'above three hundred and fifty years before' — the word of the man of God who cried against the altar at Bethel and named Josiah by name, that a child born to the house of David should burn upon it the bones of its priests, recorded at 1 Kings 13:2. What Josiah did in zeal against idolatry was, unknown to him, the exact discharge of a sentence pronounced before his great-grandfathers were born.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the mechanics of the defilement: the king caused the bones of the idolatrous priests to be taken from their graves and burnt on the very spot where the destroyed altars had stood, that he might pollute the place with the ashes of the dead — a summary, they note, of the fuller narrative at 2 Kings 23:13-14 and 2 Kings 23:16-20. Charles Ellicott, of the same school, adds that these were 'bones taken from the graves of the idolatrous priests, who were thus punished, while their altars were irreparably defiled,' and he recalls the horror with which such a violation of the dead was then regarded, citing the indignation of Amos 2:1 against Moab for burning the bones of the king of Edom. He observes too that the closing phrase, 'and cleansed Judah and Jerusalem,' does not occur at all in the parallel account, being the Chronicler's own.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns to the word behind 'the priests,' the kemarim of the Targum, the idolatrous priests distinguished from the true, and refers the reader to his note at 2 Kings 23:5. The witnesses do not divide. Gill hears the fulfilment of prophecy, Keil and Ellicott the deliberate and irreparable defilement of the high places and the Chronicler's added note of cleansing, Clarke the precise class of priests whose bones were burnt. Between them they show an act that looks merely savage until it is set against the prophetic word: the burning was not wanton but judicial, the long-delayed execution of a threat spoken over three centuries earlier, so that even the ashes on the altars testified that the God of Israel keeps his word to the letter.
6:
Josiah carries the purge beyond his own borders into the territory of the fallen northern kingdom, and the witnesses explain how a king of Judah could act so freely on Israelite soil. The reformed John Gill notes that though the cities of Manasseh, Ephraim, Simeon, and Naphtali belonged to the ten tribes, their people had been carried captive by the king of Assyria, so that the remnant left behind had become subject to the kings of Judah. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the same point at the northern extreme: Naphtali lay on the utmost border of the old kingdom of Israel, and since the ten tribes were now gone into captivity and those who had come in their stead were 'weak and few,' none could withstand the power of Josiah. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fills in the history: the cities of Israel had been ruined by the Assyrians Sargon and Shalmaneser — the latter taking Samaria after a three years' siege and deporting the people, and replacing them with foreign colonists — which is precisely what left Josiah free to desecrate the northern sanctuaries and slay their priests, as 2 Kings 23:20 records, and to destroy the great sanctuary of Bethel named at 2 Kings 23:15.

On the puzzling mention of Simeon, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch agree: the tribe is reckoned here among the northern tribes, as at 2 Chronicles 15:9, because the Simeonites, though geographically within Judah, had remained attached to the high-place worship of the north — Ellicott adding that Beersheba, a famous sanctuary in their territory, was a place of pilgrimage for the northern tribes.

A genuine textual crux runs through the verse. The obscure word the Authorised Version renders 'with their mattocks' the grammatical-historical witnesses cannot accept as it stands. Ellicott reads it rather 'in their ruins,' qualifying the cities that the Assyrians had already laid waste, and would join the whole to the next verse; Keil and Delitzsch canvass the same difficulty, noting the received text that yields no suitable sense, the marginal reading 'with their swords,' and the divergent renderings of the Septuagint, Targum, and Vulgate. Both reject the received 'mattocks.' The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke passes over the philology to the fact: even the cities under the old Israelite jurisdiction let their idols be hewn down, for 'after the truth was declared and acknowledged, the spade and the axe were employed to complete the reformation.' The witnesses converge: a depopulated and defenceless north lay open to a zealous king of Judah, who carried the cleansing to the very frontier of the land.
7:
With the northern campaign complete, the verse gathers up the whole labour and turns the king homeward — he 'beat the graven images into powder, and cut down all the idols throughout all the land of Israel, and returned to Jerusalem.' The reformed John Gill glosses only the opening, taking 'the altars and the groves' of the statues and images that stood in them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to a single word, 'the idols,' which he identifies again as the sun-statues met at v.4; the term, he notes, does not occur in the parallel account, though the sun-worship it implies is confirmed by the burning of the priests at v.5.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, read the verse as the close of one movement and the hinge to the next. Having broken down the altars and groves, beaten the images to powder, and cut down every idol throughout the land of Israel, Josiah 'returned to Jerusalem'; and then, in the eighteenth year of his reign, 'when he had purged the land and the house,' he sent Shaphan and his fellows to repair the house of the LORD his God — so that the verb of purging governs the whole and leads directly into the restoration of the temple. They dwell on the grammar of the phrase, insisting that the infinitive means neither 'after the purging' with the older expositors nor a mere statement of purpose, but marks the purging as the accomplished ground on which the repairing now proceeds.

The witnesses do not divide, and the very brevity of the notice repays a moment's weight. For six years and more the young king had ranged the length of the land — from Jerusalem north through Manasseh and Ephraim to the border of Naphtali — grinding altars to dust, felling the Asherim, burning the bones of dead priests upon their own high places. The verse sets a period to all that itinerant destruction with three plain words: he returned to Jerusalem. The negative work is done; the land and the house are purged; and the reformation, which began in the pulling down of the false, now turns to the building up of the true. What follows is no longer demolition but repair — the same zeal that had shattered the idols of the north bending itself, in the capital, to the mending of the neglected temple of God. The reader is meant to feel the turn: a kingdom cannot live by cleansing alone, and the king who has emptied the land of its idols must now fill the house with its proper worship.
8:
The eighteenth year opens the great second act of the reign, and the witnesses read the sending of the royal commissioners as the moment the reformation turns from tearing down to building up. The reformed John Gill fixes the date precisely: this was the twenty-sixth year of Josiah's age, and the purging of both land and house had been six years in the doing before it was finished. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley notes only that 'the house' is the house of God, so called by way of eminence — the one house that needs no further naming.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the whole account of the repair into a meditation on ordered, faithful work. When Josiah had purged the house of its corruptions, he began to fit it up for the services to be performed in it — and Henry turns this at once to the soul: 'Thus we must do by the spiritual temple of the heart, get it cleansed from the pollutions of sin, and then renewed, so as to be transformed into the image of God.' He marks that the king, in giving the order, calls God 'the Lord his God,' for 'those that truly love God will love the habitation of his house.' Then he traces the machinery of the work: the Levites went about the country and gathered the money, which was returned to the trustees named here and carried to Hilkiah the high priest; the funds were put into the hands of workmen, both overseers and labourers, who undertook the task 'in the gross.' Henry lingers over the care taken — the men did the work faithfully, and workmen are not truly faithful unless both careful and diligent — and over the surprising note that the overseers were skilful in instruments of music, which he takes as evidence that they were men of sense and ingenuity, their genius lying toward the mathematics that fitted them for such a trust.

Above all Henry finds in the workforce a parable of the church's varied gifts. Here were some who were bearers of burdens, cut out for bodily labour, and others of finer materials who had skill in music and were set as overseers, scribes, and officers — 'the former were the hands: these were the heads.' They had need of one another, and the work needed both; let not the overseers despise the burden-bearers, nor the labourers grudge at those whose office is to direct, but let each esteem and serve the other in love, that God may have the glory and the church the benefit. The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the year, Wesley the dignity of 'the house,' Henry the whole spirit of the enterprise — a king who, having cleansed the temple, now orders its repair with such care that the very organization of the labour becomes a lesson in the fellowship of diverse gifts under one Lord.
9:
The money gathered for the temple is delivered to the high priest, and the witnesses trace both its origin and a textual knot in the verse's last clause. The reformed John Gill notes simply that the commissioners came to Hilkiah to consult with him about the repair. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the flow of the funds: Hilkiah and the officers gave the money received for the repair to the overseers of the building, who in turn gave it to the workmen for materials and wages, exactly as had been done when the temple was repaired under Joash at 2 Chronicles 24:11-13; and they observe that the enumeration of the givers — 'from the hand of Manasseh and Ephraim, and of all the remnant of Israel' — is rhetorical, gathering the contributions of north and south into one offering for the house of God.

The crux is the closing phrase. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke argues that 'and they returned to Jerusalem' should be read 'and the inhabitants of Jerusalem,' a correction supported by many manuscripts, printed editions, and all the versions, 'as well as by necessity and common sense,' and he points to a like rectified mistake at 2 Chronicles 19:8. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reaches the same conclusion by way of the Hebrew: the received 'they returned to Jerusalem' is the marginal reading, while the Hebrew text itself has 'and the inhabitants of Jerusalem,' which is correct — the doorkeeping Levites had gathered the money of Manasseh, Ephraim, the remnant of Israel, all Judah and Benjamin, 'and the inhabitants of Jerusalem.' Keil and Delitzsch concur, calling the received correction one that grew from a misreading of the original.

So the witnesses stand together against the received text: what the Authorised Version makes a needless notice of the officers 'returning' to a city they had never left, the Hebrew and the versions make a fitting close to the list of contributors — the men of Jerusalem added to the men of the tribes. Ellicott adds that where the older narrative at 2 Kings 22:3-7 casts all this in the form of the king's instructions to Shaphan, the Chronicler tells us that those instructions were carried out. The point on which they converge is the breadth of the offering: the repair of the temple was funded not by Judah alone but by the scattered remnant of the whole covenant people, north and south together, so that the house restored was, in its very financing, the house of all Israel.
10:
The verse follows the money from the treasury into the hands that will spend it, and the witnesses attend to the chain of trust it describes. The reformed John Gill glosses the bare opening — 'they put it,' that is, the king's ministers did — passing the collected silver on to those who would direct the work. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the terms: 'the workmen' are more exactly the doers of the work, the overseers or contractors, as at 2 Chronicles 24:12; the Hebrew says that these overseers, who were working in the house of Jehovah, gave the money out for the restoring and repairing of the house, while to whom they gave it is stated only in the verse that follows. The rare verb rendered 'to repair,' he notes, occurs here only, and the whole arrangement takes its original form from 2 Kings 22:5.

Keil and Delitzsch, of the same school, unfold the whole passage as one connected description of the labour. The money was put into the hand of the overseers of the house of the LORD, who gave it to the workmen that wrought upon it, to repair and amend the house; and this same disposition of the funds — overseers first, then the artificers and builders, then the buying of stone and timber — they set beside the parallel repair under Joash, when the same careful two-stage handling of the temple money was practised.

The witnesses do not divide, and the plainness of the verse conceals a real point of religious housekeeping. The silver that had come from every quarter of the land was not handed carelessly to the first labourer, but passed through a trusted body of overseers who bore the responsibility of spending it faithfully on the house of God. So scrupulous was the arrangement that, as the older account records, no reckoning was even required of the men who handled it, because they dealt in good faith. The Chronicler dwells on this ordinary administration because, in his telling, the repair of the temple is itself an act of worship: the honest management of the offering is of a piece with the sanctity of the house it restores. Gill fixes the passing-on of the money, Ellicott the precise sense of the overseers and their office, Keil the ordered flow from trustee to workman. Between them they show a reformation that reached even into the accounts, and a people whose return to God expressed itself first in the faithful spending of a common fund upon a long-neglected house.
11:
The repair now touches the fabric of the building itself, and the witnesses read in the buying of stone and timber the measure of how far the house had fallen. The reformed John Gill takes 'the artificers and builders' plainly of the masons and carpenters, the skilled hands to whom the overseers gave the money. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the verse with care: the money went to the craftsmen and to the builders, to buy hewn stone and 'timber for the couplings' — the couplings or girders, an explanatory addition the Chronicler supplies — and 'to floor,' or rather to rafter and joist, the chambers that the kings of Judah had let fall to ruin. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agrees on this last point, glossing 'the houses' as 'the chambers joining to the temple' — the side-rooms and store-chambers that ringed the sanctuary.

The telling phrase, for the witnesses, is that these were houses 'which the kings of Judah had destroyed.' Ellicott compares the like notices of the damage done under earlier reigns — the breaking-up of the house of God by the sons of Athaliah at 2 Chronicles 24:7, and the defacements of Ahaz at 2 Chronicles 28:24 — though he allows that 'destroyed' may mean no more than 'allowed to go to ruin.' Either way the verse quietly indicts the throne itself: it was Judah's own kings, and not any foreign invader, who had brought the temple to the state that now required hewn stone and new beams.

The witnesses do not divide, and the plain inventory of building materials carries its own sober theology. The house of God had been wounded not by the enemies of Israel but by her own idolatrous rulers — by an Ahaz who shut its doors and cut up its vessels, by a Manasseh who filled it with strange altars, by an Amon who walked in his father's sins. The scars Josiah's workmen now mend are the scars left by kingship gone wrong; and the labour of stone and timber is the visible undoing of a long royal apostasy. Gill fixes the masons and carpenters, Ellicott the couplings and the raftered chambers and the guilty kings, Wesley the temple's adjoining rooms. Between them they show a king spending the people's offering to repair what other kings had ruined — a reformation that had to rebuild before it could worship, because the very house of God bore in its broken timbers the record of Judah's sin.
12:
The faithfulness of the workmen and the curious note about musical Levites draw the witnesses into the character of the labour. The reformed John Gill takes the verse plainly: the labouring men, and their inspectors too, 'did that work faithfully.' The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the phrase — literally, the men were 'dealing in good faith in the work' — and connects it to the striking notice at 2 Kings 22:7, where Josiah bids the high priest require no reckoning of the money given to the master-workmen, 'because they work in good faith.' The names of the overseers, and the details of the following verse, he observes, are peculiar to and characteristic of the Chronicler; the phrase 'to set it forward' means to lead, conduct, or preside, and is usually a musical term, as at 1 Chronicles 23:4; and the closing clause names the Levites 'every one skilled in the instruments of song,' as at 1 Chronicles 25:7.

Why musicians should oversee a building-site the witnesses take up with interest. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads it as a mark of double competence: the men named were skilful in instruments of music, and this is mentioned to intimate that, being skilful, they were exercised in both employments — they oversaw the work and also praised God with their voices and instruments. Adam Clarke, of the same school, ventures further, asking whether the musicians actually played to encourage and enliven the workmen; and he finds a parallel in the ancient fable of Amphion, whose harp was said to have raised the walls of Thebes — a story he takes, on the authority of a recovered Greek treatise on music, to preserve the memory of a real harper who played to the Theban labourers and so lightened their toil that the work went quickly forward. If that were the case here, Clarke reflects, 'instrumental music was never better applied in any thing that refers to the worship of God.'

The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Gill fixes the fidelity of the men, Ellicott the good faith that dispensed with any audit and the musical sense of the Levites' offices, Wesley their exercise in both work and worship, Clarke the pleasant conjecture that music cheered the labour. Between them they show a repair conducted not grudgingly but with song — a building-site where the guilds that sang in the temple also superintended its mending, so that the very work of restoration went forward to the sound of praise, and the honesty of the workmen was such that the king's treasury asked no account of them at all.
13:
The organization of the labour is completed here, with the Levites set over the burden-bearers and staffing the offices of the work, and the witnesses draw out the dignity of their several charges. The reformed John Gill explains the oversight of 'the bearers of burdens' as a practical necessity: these Levites looked after the men who carried the timber and the stones, to see that they were not dilatory, and that the workmen might never stand idle for want of materials brought to their hands. The whole enterprise, on his reading, was kept moving by attentive foremen who matched supply to labour.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fastens on the honour the verse assigns to the musical guilds of Levites. They who were skilled in the instruments of song were set over the burden-bearers, and probably, he suggests, 'cheered their labours with song and music, as was the practice in ancient Egypt' — the overseers being, as at v.12, leaders and conductors of the work. He notes further that the Levites furnished not only musicians but scribes, officers, and porters for the business of the restoration, comparing the ordering of the Levitical service at 1 Chronicles 23:4-5, and tracing the guild of scribes back to 1 Chronicles 2:55; the writer may intend only to say that there were Levitical guilds of these officers as well as of singers.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse, dry as it looks, discloses the Chronicler's abiding interest — the honourable and ordered service of the Levites in every part of the house of God. It was not beneath the temple singers to superintend the hauling of stone; the same men who led the praise led the porters and the labourers, so that the mending of the fabric was as much a Levitical ministry as the music that would one day fill it. Gill fixes the diligence of the foremen, Ellicott the varied offices and the dignity of the musical guilds. Between them they show a work-site governed not by hired taskmasters but by the consecrated tribe, in which scribes, officers, porters, burden-bearers, and singers each had a place, and the repair of the sanctuary was carried on as a single, ordered act of worship — every hand, from the hauler of stone to the master of song, set in its appointed rank under the God whose house they were making whole.
14:
The turning-point of the whole chapter comes almost by accident, in the routine handling of the temple money — 'Hilkiah the priest found a book of the law of the LORD given by Moses.' The reformed John Gill traces the circumstance: as the Levites brought out the money that had been gathered from the country into the temple, and passed it on through the high priest and the king's ministers to the overseers, the repairs were set going, and in that bringing-out the book was found. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch are careful about what the words do and do not say: it is not clearly implied that Hilkiah found the book in the place where the money was laid up; and the volume is characterized as the book of the Mosaic law by the phrase 'by the hand of Moses,' without necessarily being Moses' own autograph.

Charles Ellicott, of the same school, notes that this verse is not in the book of Kings but supplements the older account by assigning the occasion of the discovery. He gathers the traditions: Josephus has Hilkiah find the book in the treasure-chamber he had entered to fetch gold and silver for sacred vessels, while Rabbinical tradition held it had lain hidden under a heap of stones, placed there to save it from being burnt by Ahaz. The phrase 'given by Moses,' he adds, belongs strictly not to 'the book' but to 'the law of Jehovah' — the law communicated through the instrumentality of Moses, as at 2 Chronicles 33:8.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, refusing to add to the well-known narrative, turns instead to thanksgiving over the very thing Josiah lacked. 'We may hence take occasion to bless God that we have plenty of Bibles, and that they are, or may be, in all hands' — that the book of the law and gospel is not lost, is not scarce, so that in this sense 'the word of the Lord is not precious.' Bibles are jewels, he says, but thanks be to God they are not rarities; the fountain of the waters of life is not a spring shut up but streams that make glad the city of God. And he draws the sharp application: 'what a great deal shall we have to answer for if the great things of God's law, being thus made common, should be accounted by us as strange things!' The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, for his part, simply refers the reader to the fuller notice at 2 Kings 22:8. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the occasion and the traditions of the finding, Keil the careful sense of 'the book of the law given by Moses,' Henry the wonder that a book once lost in the very house of God is now in every hand. Between them they mark the moment a buried book surfaced to reshape a kingdom — and the reader is left to weigh whether the abundance of the word among us breeds reverence or contempt.
29:
The king, having heard both the law and the prophetess, gathers the whole nation to renew its covenant with God, and the witnesses read the assembly as the crown of the reformation. The reformed John Gill notes only that from this point to the end of the chapter the Chronicler gives the same account of the reading of the law to the people, and of the covenant king and people made to serve the LORD, as is found in the parallel at 2 Kings 23.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the further advances Josiah now made upon the message God had sent him. 'Happy the people that had such a king,' he says, for they were first well taught: the king did not go about to force them to their duty until he had instructed them in it, calling all the people together, great and small, rich and poor, high and low, that all might hear the words of the book of the covenant which concerned them all. Then they were well fixed: the articles of agreement between God and Israel being read, both king and people solemnly subscribed them, the king covenanting in his place to keep God's commandments with all his heart and soul, and urging the people to declare their consent likewise, until he had made them all to serve, 'even to serve the Lord their God.' And then they were well tended: all Josiah's days they departed not from following the LORD, though it was with much ado that he kept them from running into idolatry again.

Yet Henry will not gild the reformation, and here he reads its tragic underside. All Josiah's days were days of restraint upon a people whose hearts still leaned to their idols; many wanted nothing but to have the good king out of the way, and then their high places and images would be up again. He points to the witness of the prophets who lived through it — that in these very years God charged treacherous Judah with returning to him only feignedly, and that from the beginning of Josiah's reformation the iniquity of the house of Judah was dated that would bring on its ruin, as Jeremiah 3:6 and Ezekiel 4:6 attest. The king was sincere, but the generality of the people were averse; and nothing, Henry warns, hastens the ruin of a people more than the baffling of hopeful reformation by a hypocritical return to God — 'be not deceived, God is not mocked.' The witnesses do not divide. Gill refers the account to its parallel; Henry reads in the great assembly both the height of Josiah's work and the hidden reason it could not, in the end, save a people whose repentance was only skin-deep.
33:
The chapter closes with a summary of Josiah's whole work and a guarded verdict on its endurance — 'he made all that were present in Israel to serve the LORD their God,' and 'all his days they departed not.' The reformed John Gill takes the opening plainly: Josiah took away all the abominations, all the idols, out of every country that pertained to the children of Israel, gathering up in a sentence the destruction related at length through the chapter. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that 'out of all the countries' means out of the territories of the ten tribes, so that the notice glances back to the northern campaign of v.6 and summarises the abolition of the heathen worships. He marks the peculiar phrase 'made to serve, even to serve,' a construction unique to the Chronicler, and confesses the style of the whole verse to be his.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley seizes on that very repetition, 'even to serve,' and reads in it the singleness of the king's aim: the doubling shows 'that this was the only thing his heart was set upon. He aimed at nothing in all he did but to engage them to God and their duty.' The whole labour of the reign — the purging, the repairing, the covenanting — had this one end, to bring the people into the true service of the LORD.

Yet the witnesses do not let the triumph stand unqualified, for the verse itself does not. Ellicott hears in 'all his days they departed not' the honest measure of a reformation by royal mandate: the king's will secured an outward conformity to the legitimate worship, and open idolatry was, for the time, a peril too serious to be risked; but the unreality of these reforms is proved, he says, by the relapse that followed immediately upon Josiah's death, and by the moral corruption then preying upon the nation's vitals, which the pages of Jeremiah lay bare. The people served the LORD all Josiah's days — but it was his days, and his will, that held them to it. Gill fixes the sweep of the cleansing; Wesley the singleness of the king's heart; Ellicott the sober truth that a nation's outward conformity is not the same as its inward return. Between them they close the chapter where it began, on a king wholly given to God — and on a people whose obedience, real while he lived, would not outlast the hand that compelled it.
2:
The Chronicler's one-line verdict on Josiah is unusually absolute, and the witnesses feel its weight. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that the encomium 'he declined neither to the right hand, nor to the left' is pronounced of no other king; it is, in effect, to say that his observance of the law was perfect, and Ellicott sets it beside the very charge laid on Israel and on her kings in Deuteronomy 5:32, Deuteronomy 17:20, and Deuteronomy 28:14, where to turn aside neither to right nor left is the whole duty of the king under the covenant.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws the moral portrait out of the metaphor. Josiah 'never swerved from God and truth; he never omitted what he knew to be his duty'; he carried on his reformation with a steady hand, so that timidity did not keep him from going far enough, and zeal did not carry him beyond due bounds. He walked, Clarke says, in the golden mean, and his moderation was known unto all men — he went neither to the right nor to the left, but 'looked inward, looked forward, and looked upward.' Clarke turns from exposition to appeal: 'let the conduct of this pious youth be thy exemplar through life.'

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch bind this verdict to what follows, reading the verse together with the next as a single movement: because he walked in the ways of David his father and turned neither way, therefore in the eighth year, while yet a youth of sixteen, he began to seek the God of that same David, and in the twelfth year to purge Judah and Jerusalem. The rightness of the reign is not an abstract commendation but the root of the concrete reformation the chapter will unfold. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott fixes the uniqueness of the praise and its rootage in the law of the king; Clarke reads it as steadiness and balance, a zeal without excess and a caution without cowardice; Keil makes it the seed of the seeking and the purging to come. Between them they show why the historian, who measures every king of Judah against David, gives to Josiah alone the unqualified word: here at last was a king who kept the road exactly, bending neither toward the idolatry on the one hand nor toward a lawless zeal on the other, and whose whole reign was the working-out of that single, unswerving fidelity.
15:
The found book begins its journey from the sanctuary to the throne, and the witness follows the quiet handoff that would shake a kingdom. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the first link in the chain: Hilkiah answered and said to Shaphan the scribe, 'I have found the book of the law in the house of the LORD,' and delivered the book into Shaphan's hand. The high priest does not carry it himself to the king; he entrusts it to the royal secretary, the officer whose place it was to bring the temple's business before the crown.

Keil and Delitzsch set this verse at the head of a whole movement, reading the section that follows as the account of how the discovery was communicated — by the high priest to the state secretary, and by him to the king — and how the king was dismayed at what he heard and sent to inquire of the prophetess Huldah concerning the judgments the law threatened. The whole, they note, runs closely parallel to the older narrative at 2 Kings 22:8-10, so that the two accounts may be read together, each confirming the other. They stress that the records here agree throughout, the Chronicler abridging nothing of substance; and they take Hilkiah's calm announcement as the sober faith of a priest who knows what he holds — not a curiosity of antiquity but the covenant charter of the nation, mislaid in its own house.

The witness leaves the verse in its plainness, and the plainness is itself eloquent. Hilkiah's words are the announcement of a recovery: 'I have found' — as of a thing lost and long sought, now restored to the house where it belonged. That the book of the law should have to be 'found' in the temple is the measure of how far Judah had fallen under Manasseh and Amon; that it is found precisely now, as Josiah's cleansing and repairing reach their height, is the measure of the providence that governs the reign. The book passes from priest to scribe with no sign yet of the storm it carries; Hilkiah states the fact, delivers the volume, and the narrative moves on. But everything that follows — the reading before the king, the rent garments, the errand to Huldah, the great covenant of the closing verses — hangs upon this modest transaction. The word of God, long silent in its own sanctuary, has been put back into circulation; and from the moment it leaves the high priest's hand for the scribe's, the reformation ceases to be merely the king's project and becomes the book's.
20:
The stricken king does not despair but sends at once for a word from the LORD, and the witness records the delegation he dispatches. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the commission: Josiah commanded Hilkiah the high priest, and Ahikam the son of Shaphan, and Abdon the son of Micah, and Shaphan the scribe, and Asaiah a servant of the king's, charging them to go and inquire of the LORD for him and for the people concerning the words of the book that had been found. The reading of these verses, they note, runs parallel throughout to the older account at 2 Kings 22:12, where the same men are named as the king's messengers.

The composition of the embassy is itself instructive, and the witness lets it stand in its dignity. Josiah does not send a single courier but a weighty deputation drawn from the highest ranks of his kingdom: the high priest himself, the son of the very scribe who had read the book, a royal officer, the scribe Shaphan, and a trusted servant of the king. The gravity of the errand is measured by the rank of those sent on it — a king who has heard the law and trembled will not entrust the inquiry to any lesser hands.

Above all the verse marks the instinct of a truly pious king in the hour of alarm. Josiah has just learned, from the book's own curses, how great is the danger hanging over Judah; and his first act is not to defend himself, nor to explain away the threat, nor to redouble his reforms in his own strength, but to 'inquire of the LORD.' He seeks a word from God about the word of God — asking not whether the book is true, which he does not doubt, but what its threatenings mean for him and his people now. The witness leaves the verse as the hinge between the king's dismay and the prophetess's answer: the rent garments of the previous verse become the sent embassy of this one, terror turning at once into supplication. Keil and Delitzsch fix the names and the parallel; and in the naming the reader sees a throne that, confronted by the wrath of heaven, knew of nothing better to do than to ask heaven what it required. The reformation, begun in zeal against idols, has become a reign that seeks the mind of God before it acts.
30:
The covenant is renewed in the house of the LORD, with the whole people gathered to hear the book read, and the witnesses attend to the assembly and a notable textual change. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set out the scene as the Chronicler gives it: the king went up into the house of the LORD, and with him all the men of Judah, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the priests and the Levites, and all the people, great and small; and he read in their ears all the words of the book of the covenant that had been found in the house of the LORD. This reading, they note, leads directly into the king's own covenanting and the binding of the people, the whole forming one solemn act of national return.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke touches the verse only to refer the reader to his note on the parallel at 2 Kings 23:1, where the same going-up is related. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes on a single difference from the older account: where Kings names 'the prophets' among the assembled, the Chronicler has 'the Levites.' It was a natural change to make, Ellicott suggests, seeing that the prophetic order had long been extinct in the Chronicler's own day; it may even be the result of an unconscious error, since the phrase 'priests and Levites' recurs so constantly in his pages that his pen ran to it of itself.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse gathers the whole reformation into one great congregation. Everything the king had done in private — his seeking of God, his purging of the land, his repairing of the house, his terror at the law and his errand to Huldah — now becomes the act of the whole people, summoned into the temple to hear for themselves the book that had shaken their king. That Josiah himself read it aloud, as the following verses show, gave the service its weight: the crown did not delegate the word but delivered it in person. Keil fixes the sweep of the assembly, great and small; Clarke points to the fuller account in Kings; Ellicott marks the Chronicler's telling substitution of Levites for prophets, a small window onto the age in which he wrote. Between them they show a kingdom brought bodily before the recovered word of God — the reading that had broken one heart now set before the hearts of all.
22:
The embassy seeks out a prophetess, and the witnesses attend both to her person and to the tangled text that names her. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke passes over the details to the fact, identifying Huldah simply as the prophetess and referring the reader to his fuller note at 2 Kings 22:14. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott works patiently at the wording. The clause 'and they that the king had appointed' rests on a defective Hebrew text, which he would restore from the versions — the Septuagint's 'they whom the king had commanded,' or better the Syriac and Vulgate's 'all they whom the king sent' — noting that three manuscripts read 'the king's princes,' a plausible correction, and that the older account at 2 Kings 22:14 supplies the names already given above.

Ellicott traces the variants in Huldah's genealogy: her husband Shallum is 'son of Tikvath' — the Chronicler's Tukahath — where Kings has Tikvah, the Septuagint, Syriac, and Vulgate confirming the reading; and 'son of Hasrah' where Kings has Harhas, the versions again dividing. He locates her dwelling 'in the college,' which he takes to mean the second quarter, the lower city of Jerusalem, and marks the phrase 'to that effect' as the Chronicler's own addition. The differences in the text of the oracle that follows, he adds, are mostly due to alteration of the original, which is more exactly preserved in Kings.

The witnesses do not divide, and the choice of Huldah is itself the quiet wonder of the passage. The high priest, the scribe, and the king's officers — the greatest men of the realm, sent by a king in terror — do not go to some famous prophet but to a woman living in a quarter of Jerusalem, the wife of the keeper of the wardrobe; and to her word they submit the fate of the kingdom. Clarke fixes her office and points to the fuller notice in Kings; Ellicott secures her name and dwelling against the corruptions of the text. Between them they show a court that, seeking the mind of the LORD, cared nothing for the rank or sex of his messenger but only that the message be his. The men that the king had sent came to Huldah and spoke to her the charge they bore; and the reader waits, with the trembling embassy, for the answer of God through the mouth of the prophetess.
27:
The reason for the king's exemption is his tender and humbled heart, and the witnesses draw out both the words and their weight. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke turns to the Targum's rendering of the verse: 'because thy heart was melted, and thou hast humbled thyself in the sight of the Word of the Lord' — the meymera — 'when thou didst hear his words,' the pithgamoi, 'against this place.' Clarke fastens on the distinction the paraphrase preserves, between the meymera, the personal Word of the Lord, and the pithgam, the word spoken or expressed; the Targum, he observes, 'most evidently distinguishes' the two — the living Word before whom Josiah humbled himself, and the uttered words of the book that he had heard. It is a small philological note that opens, for later readers, upon the great mystery of the Word who is himself a Person.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the encouragement of the whole passage: we are here moved to humble ourselves before God and seek unto him, as Josiah did — for even if we cannot prevail thereby to turn away God's wrath from our land, yet we shall thereby deliver our own souls. The rending of the garments and the melting of the heart were not lost; God was well pleased with them, and answered them with a personal promise of peace. The tenderness that could not save the kingdom saved the king.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse fixes the ground of all such mercy. Josiah is spared not for the greatness of his reforms — though no king had done more — but for the tenderness of his heart and the depth of his humbling; God looks first upon the melted heart. Clarke hears in the Targum's careful words the personal Word of the Lord before whom the king bowed; Henry hears the summons to every reader to humble himself likewise and so deliver his own soul. Between them they show the meeting of two things the chapter has held in tension — an unquenchable wrath against a place, and an open ear toward a penitent — resolved in the person of a king who trembled at the word. The God who had just pronounced doom upon Jerusalem stoops to say, 'I have heard thee also'; and the reader learns that no genuine humbling before God is ever overlooked, however far gone the nation in which it is found.
28:
The personal promise is completed here — the king shall be gathered to his grave in peace, and shall not see the evil to come — and the witnesses read it as mercy, though a mercy shadowed by what history would bring. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke touches the verse lightly, referring the reader to his fuller note on the parallel at 2 Kings 22:20, where the meaning of being 'gathered to thy grave in peace' is drawn out. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the promise the chapter's great comfort: good people are here taught to be so far from fearing death as rather to welcome it when it takes them away from the evil to come. See, he says, how the property of death is altered by making it the matter of a promise — 'thou shalt be gathered to thy grave in peace,' housed in that ark, as Noah was, when a deluge is coming upon the world.

The witnesses do not divide, and the tenderness of the word is unmistakable: the king who wept at the law is promised that he shall be spared the sight of the ruin his own eyes had foreseen. Yet the phrase 'in peace' carries a difficulty the attentive reader cannot miss, for Josiah did not die quietly in his bed but fell wounded on the field of Megiddo, as 2 Chronicles 35:24 will record. The promise is not of a painless death but of a merciful one — that he should be gathered to his fathers and laid in his grave before the curses of the book fell upon Jerusalem, taken away, like the righteous of Isaiah 57:1, from the evil to come. To be buried in peace, in the idiom of the book, is to be spared the desolation, not to be spared the sword.

Clarke points to the fuller exposition in Kings; Henry lifts the promise into a doctrine of the believer's death, welcomed as a gathering-in before the flood. Between them they show the last word of the oracle to be pure grace: a king cannot, by his tenderness, unmake a nation's doom, but he can be hidden from it. Josiah's reward for a melted heart is not the salvation of Judah, which was past saving, but the mercy of an early grave — that he should sleep with his fathers before the deluge broke, and not live to watch the house he had repaired go up in flame. The embassy that went out in terror returns with this: judgment for the place, and for the penitent king, peace.
31:
The king takes his stand and binds himself by covenant to the LORD, and the witnesses attend to the place where he stood and the solemnity of the act. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke refers the reader to his notes on the parallel at 2 Kings 23:3, and on the preceding chapter, for the circumstances of the covenant here gathered up. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the phrase 'in his place' more exactly as 'on his stand' — the same station named at 2 Chronicles 23:13, which the Authorised Version there renders 'at his pillar' — where the older account has a word that appears to be synonymous, 'on the dais.' The covenant, he notes, is properly 'the covenant,' the definite article marking it as the covenant of the law just read.

The station is worth marking, for it carries a quiet echo. The pillar or dais on which Josiah now stands to pledge his obedience is the very place where, generations before, the boy-king Joash had stood at his coronation to be shown to the people, as 2 Chronicles 23:13 records. The royal station that had once witnessed the crowning of a king now witnesses a king's submission to a higher throne; Josiah takes the place of majesty only to bind himself, in the sight of all, to walk after the LORD and to keep his commandments, his testimonies, and his statutes with all his heart and soul.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse fixes the true order of the reformation. The king does not command the people to covenant before he has covenanted himself; he stands first in his own place and pledges his own obedience 'to perform the words of the covenant which are written in this book.' The reform is not imposed from above upon a reluctant people while the throne holds itself aloof; it begins with the king's personal engagement, made publicly and by name. Ellicott's cross-reference to the same 'stand' at the crowning of Joash is not idle antiquarianism; the Chronicler, who alone preserves that earlier scene, sets Josiah on the identical spot, so that the reader who knows the history sees one king made on that dais and another there kneeling in submission, bowing before a higher throne on the very platform of his own majesty. Clarke gathers the circumstances from the parallel; Ellicott secures the sense of the royal station and the definite covenant. Between them they show a monarch who, having read the book to the people, is the first to submit to it — leading his kingdom back to God not by decree only but by the example of his own vow, taken openly on the dais where kings are made.
32:
The king now binds the people to the covenant he has himself embraced, and the witnesses attend both to the act and to a knot in the text. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the phrase 'to stand to it' as a public gesture: it is likely, he says, that Josiah caused all the assembly to arise when he read the terms of the covenant, and thus by standing to testify their approbation of it and their resolution to observe it faithfully and perseveringly. John Wesley, of the same school, takes it that the king 'caused them to engage by an oath or covenant that they would observe the laws of God, as his predecessors had formerly done, and which indeed they were before obliged to do' — the covenant adding no new duty, but binding afresh the duty they already owed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott works at the Hebrew. Where the Chronicler writes that the king 'caused all present to stand to it,' the older account at the parallel place says that 'all the people stood into,' that is, came into, the covenant; the two readings, he notes, differ only in the vowels, which anciently were not written, so that 'he stood' and 'he caused to stand' were one in the unpointed text. He judges the phrase 'all that were present in Jerusalem and Benjamin' unusual, and suspects that 'and Benjamin' is really a corruption of the words 'into the covenant,' which the sense requires here as much as in Kings; and he marks the closing clause, that the inhabitants of Jerusalem did according to the covenant of God, as the Chronicler's own addition, recording that they acted upon the oath after they had solemnly taken it upon themselves.

The witnesses do not divide over the substance. Clarke and Wesley fix the outward act — the people rising to their feet to pledge, by oath, an obedience they already owed; Ellicott secures the wording against the corruptions of the text and marks the Chronicler's note that the pledge was kept, at least outwardly, in the doing. Between them they show the covenant descending from the king to the nation: what Josiah had vowed on his own stand, the people now ratify on their feet, and the assembly that had gathered to hear the book departs bound by oath to keep it. The reformation has become, for a moment at least, the sworn act of a whole people — a unanimity the closing verse will both celebrate and, in its guarded phrasing, quietly qualify.
16:
Shaphan carries the book to the king, but not before he renders his account of the work, and the witnesses attend to the report and its wording. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott clarifies the phrasing: 'carried' is rather 'brought in,' and 'brought the king word again' means further, or besides; the money 'committed to thy servants' was given into the hand of the servants — that is, the overseers of the repairs — and 'they do it' should read 'they are doing it,' the work being still in hand. He notes that the clause 'Shaphan brought the book in unto the king' is only a different pointing of the words 'Shaphan the scribe came in unto the king' at 2 Kings 22:9, the rest of the verse being an addition of the Chronicler's.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh the same difference and find in it no discrepancy. Where the Chronicler writes 'And Shaphan brought the book to the king,' instead of the words of Kings, 'and Shaphan the scribe came to the king,' the change 'involves no difference as to the facts; it rather makes the matter clear' — the Chronicler simply naming outright the book that Shaphan carried in his hand. The two witnesses of the same school thus agree that the accounts, for all their small verbal divergence, tell one story.

The order of Shaphan's report is itself worth marking, and the witnesses let it stand. The scribe comes before the king first with the ordinary business — the money faithfully gathered and delivered, the repairs going forward under trusty hands — and only afterward, almost as an afterthought, with the extraordinary thing that had been found. The stewardship is discharged before the discovery is disclosed; the servant renders his account of the lesser matter before he unfolds the greater. There is a fittingness in it: the reformation had begun in the honest management of a common fund, and it is out of that faithful ordinary labour, the repairing of a neglected house, that the great thing emerges. Ellicott adds that the notes bearing on the handling of the temple money at the like repairs of Joash may apply here as well, pointing back to 2 Kings 12:11 and 2 Chronicles 24:11 — so ordinary and familiar was the machinery of stewardship the scribe describes. Ellicott fixes the sense of the report and its relation to the older text, Keil the harmony of the two accounts. Between them they show the book making its way, by the plainest official channels, from the priest's hand through the scribe's report to the ear of a king who does not yet know what he is about to hear.
17:
Before the book is so much as named, Shaphan reports that the temple fund has been faithfully discharged, and the witnesses attend to the emptying of the chest. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders 'gathered together' more exactly as 'poured out' — the money poured out from the chest or chests in which it had been collected — and points to 2 Kings 22:9, where 'the doers of the work' are identified with the overseers. The closing phrase, 'and to the hand of the workmen,' he suggests may be explanatory, the conjunction meaning 'even' or 'that is,' so that the overseers and the workmen who received the silver are one and the same body of trusted men.

Keil and Delitzsch, tracing Shaphan's back-report to the king, include this verse in the communication that runs from the finding of the book to its reading, narrated here just as in the older account of 2 Kings 22:8-10. The scribe's word is a word of stewardship: the money that had been found and gathered in the house of the LORD has been counted out and delivered into the hands appointed to spend it, exactly as the king commanded.

The witnesses do not divide, and the verse, slight as it is, keeps the reformation grounded in the ordinary. The great drama of the found book is about to break; but first the accounts must be squared. Shaphan reports that nothing has miscarried — the offering of the tribes and of Jerusalem has been poured out of the chest and put into faithful hands, the repairs are funded and proceeding, the king's charge is fulfilled. It is the same scrupulous handling that marked the repair under Joash, when the temple silver passed in careful stages from collectors to overseers to craftsmen. Only when this lesser matter is settled does the scribe turn to the thing that will overturn the king. The doers of the work and the workmen being, on Ellicott's reading, one and the same body, the verse describes a single trusted company that both oversaw and executed the repair, so that the money passed through the fewest possible hands — a further safeguard of the honest handling the older account had so warmly praised. Ellicott fixes the poured-out silver and the identity of the overseers and workmen; Keil sets the notice within Shaphan's faithful report. Between them they show a kingdom whose return to God expressed itself first in honest bookkeeping — the money accounted for, the work advancing — so that the extraordinary word, when it comes, comes to a court that has just proved itself faithful in a very little.
18:
Now at last the scribe names the book and reads it aloud, and the witnesses mark both the plainness of the notice and a temptation to over-read it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott observes that the verse is all but identical with 2 Kings 22:10, save that where the older account says Shaphan 'read it' before the king, the Chronicler writes that he 'read in it' — a phrase which may mean the very same thing. He cautions against the guess that the Chronicler altered the words on purpose 'in order to insinuate that the book was of considerable size'; the change, he judges, is too slight to bear such weight.

Keil and Delitzsch had already prepared this moment in their account of the discovery, taking the reading before the king as the culmination of the chain by which the found book passed from Hilkiah to Shaphan and from Shaphan to Josiah — the whole communicated, they note, just as at 2 Kings 22:8-10. The scribe's brief announcement, 'Hilkiah the priest hath given me a book,' is the hinge; and then, without ceremony, 'Shaphan read it before the king.'

The witnesses do not divide, and the restraint of the verse is its power. There is no description of the scene, no record of the king's face as he listened — only the flat statement that the scribe read, and the reader is left to imagine the words of the law falling for the first time in living memory upon the ear of a king who had sought God from his youth but had never, perhaps, heard the book entire. Whether it was the whole law of Moses or the roll of Deuteronomy with its terrible curses, the witnesses do not finally determine; Ellicott will not build a theory of its bulk upon a single altered preposition. What they leave standing is the bare, momentous fact: the word of God, so long lost that its recovery was news, is now read aloud in the palace of Judah. The next verse will record what that reading did. That the scribe, and not the priest or the king, is the one to read marks the office of Shaphan as the reader of state documents before the crown; the found book is treated, at least at first, as one more roll to be reported and read in the ordinary course of business — which makes the king's extraordinary reaction, in the verse that follows, the more arresting. Ellicott secures the wording against over-interpretation, Keil the place of the reading in the whole movement of the discovery. Between them they bring the book to the point of its impact — read, at last, in the hearing of the king whose heart it was about to break.
21:
The content of the king's charge is given here, and the witnesses attend to its wording and its wide compassion — 'Go, inquire of the LORD for me, and for them that are left in Israel and in Judah.' The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes that the verse is virtually identical with 2 Kings 22:13, but that the Chronicler has altered its phrasing in two telling ways. Where Kings has 'for the people and for all Judah,' the Chronicler writes 'for them that are left in Israel and in Judah' — thinking, Ellicott says, of the remnant left in the northern kingdom after the Assyrian deportations, the survivors whom Josiah's reforms had reached. And where Kings says the wrath of the LORD is 'kindled against' Judah, the Chronicler writes that it is 'poured out upon us' — a change, Ellicott suggests, that betrays a writer who 'remembered the ruin of the ten tribes,' the wrath he names having already fallen upon the north.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the king's errand as the pattern of every awakened conscience. When we are under convictions of sin and apprehensions of divine wrath, Henry says, we are here directed to inquire of the Lord, as Josiah did; it concerns us to ask, with those pricked in heart, 'Men and brethren, what shall we do?' — and, like the trembling jailer, 'What must I do to be saved?' The king does not merely grieve over the threatened judgment; he seeks to know the mind of God upon it, that he may do whatever the word requires.

The witnesses converge on the breadth and the humility of the inquiry. Ellicott fixes the Chronicler's tender enlargement of the phrase to include the scattered remnant of the north, and his solemn substitution of wrath 'poured out' for wrath 'kindled,' as of one writing after the catastrophe had come; Henry draws the abiding lesson that conviction of sin should drive the soul to inquire of God rather than to flee from him. Between them they show a king whose alarm reached beyond his own throne to embrace 'all that are left' of the covenant people, north and south together, and who answered the terror of the law not with despair but with a question laid before the LORD. The verse gathers the whole penitence of Josiah into a single movement: he has heard the wrath, he owns it as poured out upon 'us,' and he sends to learn what a God so provoked will now require of a remnant so nearly consumed.
24:
Huldah's answer opens with unrelieved judgment upon the place — 'Behold, I will bring evil upon this place, and upon the inhabitants thereof, even all the curses that are written in the book.' The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the tense: the words are strictly 'I am about to bring,' a participle of imminent action, so that the doom is not distant but at the door. And he marks the Chronicler's characteristic phrasing — 'all the curses that are written in the book' is an explanatory paraphrase of the older account's 'all the words of the book'; the prophetess reads the threatened evil as the very curses of the law, and Ellicott points the reader to their catalogue in Deuteronomy, the curses of Deuteronomy 28:16 and following and the covenant sanctions of Deuteronomy 29:20, and the great reading of blessing and curse at Joshua 8:34.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the oracle a standing warning to nations. We are here warned, he says, of the ruin that sin brings upon kingdoms: those who forsake God bring evil upon themselves and 'kindle a fire which shall not be quenched.' Such, Henry adds, will the fire of God's wrath be when the decree has gone forth against a people that obstinately and impenitently persist in their wicked ways — the very sentence now pronounced over Judah.

The witnesses do not divide, and the force of the verse lies in what it does not spare. Huldah, given the chance to soften the book before a king who had done more against idolatry than any of his fathers, does not soften it at all: the evil is coming, the curses are written, the place and its people lie under sentence. The law that Josiah had heard read is confirmed, word for word, by the living voice of prophecy; the threatenings are not rhetoric but the fixed purpose of God against a nation's long apostasy. Ellicott's train of Deuteronomic references — the curses of the covenant, the sanctions of the great renewal, the reading of blessing and cursing upon the mountains — shows that Huldah is not inventing a new doom but reading back to the king the very sanctions of the book he had just heard, so that prophecy and law speak with one voice. Ellicott fixes the imminence of the doom and its identity with the Deuteronomic curses; Henry draws the lesson that forsaking God kindles an unquenchable fire. Between them they show that the reformation, real as it was, had come too late to turn away the wrath earned by generations — and yet the very next verses will show that a tender heart, though it cannot save the place, is not overlooked by the God who sentences it.
25:
The ground of the sentence is named — 'because they have forsaken me, and have burned incense unto other gods' — and the witnesses weigh the charge and its unquenchable penalty. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the wording. Where the older account reads that they provoked the LORD 'with all the work of their hands,' several manuscripts and the Syriac agree with the Chronicler's plural, 'works'; and where Kings says the wrath 'shall be kindled,' the Chronicler again writes that it is 'poured out' — though Ellicott observes that the reading of Kings, 'kindled,' agrees better with the following clause, 'and shall not be quenched,' the same alteration he had marked at v.21. He notes too that the verb rendered 'burned incense' stands here in the causative form, which is commoner in the Chronicle than the form used in Kings.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse with the one before it as a single warning of national ruin: those who forsake God bring evil upon themselves and kindle a fire that shall not be quenched. The image is the prophetess's own — a wrath 'poured out' and yet burning, a fire no reformation now could put out — and Henry takes it as the sober end of a people that has persisted in provoking God with the works of its hands.

The witnesses do not divide, and the theology of the verse is exact. The evil is not arbitrary but earned: Judah is judged for two things named together — forsaking the LORD and burning incense to other gods, the abandonment and the substitution that are the very heart of idolatry. The wrath is 'poured out,' as of a vessel emptied and not to be recalled, and 'shall not be quenched,' as of a fire that has caught past all putting-out. Yet the reader who has followed the chapter knows what Huldah is about to add: that this same unquenchable wrath, fixed against the place, will nonetheless pass over the head of the one king who trembled at it. The plural 'works of their hands,' which Ellicott finds supported against the singular of Kings, widens the charge from a single idol to the whole manufacture of a nation's false worship — every image and altar the reforming king had ground to dust; and the wrath 'poured out' answers, in its very verb, the incense the people had poured out to other gods. Ellicott fixes the textual shading of 'works' and 'poured out' and the grammar of the incense; Henry the lesson of a fire kindled by apostasy. Between them they show a judgment grounded in justice and beyond recall — the necessary dark against which the mercy of the following verses will shine all the brighter.
26:
The oracle turns from the doomed place to the trembling king, and the witness follows the pivot in its very grammar. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks the shift: 'as for the king of Judah, who sent you to inquire of the LORD,' the prophetess now addresses a personal word to Josiah himself. He renders the phrase 'to inquire of the LORD' more strictly as 'through the LORD,' where Kings has the accusative; and he notes the Chronicler's characteristic additions and refinements throughout the verse. The clause 'and humbledst thyself before me' is not in the older account — a repetition, Ellicott observes, in the Chronicler's manner, anticipating the fuller word of the next verse; and where Kings threatens simply that God will bring evil 'against this place,' adding 'that it should become an astonishment and a curse,' the Chronicler shapes the sentence to his own ends.

Ellicott gathers the smaller marks of the Chronicler's hand: the shorter form of the verb 'and weep,' a correction of the longer word in Kings; the emphatic 'I' where the older text has its fuller form; the solemn 'saith the LORD,' the utterance of Jehovah; the plural 'graves' for the singular, as at 2 Chronicles 16:14; and the clause 'and upon the inhabitants of the same,' added by the Chronicler to the promise. Each small change, in his reading, is the trace of a writer retelling the oracle in his own idiom while keeping its substance whole.

The witness leaves the verse poised on its great reversal, and the reversal is the heart of it. Huldah has just pronounced an unquenchable wrath upon the place and its people; now, with a single turn — 'as for the king' — she singles out one man for a wholly different word. The God who will not spare Jerusalem will spare Josiah; the same message carries doom to the nation and mercy to the penitent within it. The Chronicler's very additions, his 'humbledst thyself' and his 'saith the LORD,' press the point that this personal word is as sure as the sentence it follows. Ellicott fixes the pivot and the philology of the Chronicler's retelling. What the verse announces, and the next unfolds, is that the wrath of God against a place and the tenderness of God toward a broken heart are not at odds: the one king who wept at the word is met, in the midst of a doomed kingdom, by a promise made to him alone.
19:
The reading of the law strikes the king to the heart, and he rends his garments — the one gesture the verse records, and the witnesses read it as the true measure of Josiah's piety. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley makes the king's shock a mirror for the reader: 'were the things contained in scripture new to us, as they were here to Josiah, surely they would make deeper impressions upon us than they commonly do.' They are not the less weighty, Wesley urges, and should not be the less regarded, because they are well known — the very familiarity that dulls us was the thing Josiah did not have to blunt the word's edge.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same lesson from the rent clothes. When the king heard the words of the law he rent his garments, and God, as the later verses show, was well pleased with his doing so; from which Henry bids us, whenever we read or hear the word of God, to affect our hearts with it and to possess them with a holy fear of that wrath against all ungodliness which the scripture reveals — the wrath that made Josiah's tender heart tremble. Yet Henry turns the gesture inward: 'Rend the heart therefore, and not the garments.' The tearing of the robe was acceptable only because it expressed a torn heart; the outward sign is nothing without the inward grief it signifies.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch name the emotion plainly as 'the dismay of the king at the contents of the book which was read to him' — a dismay that will drive him at once to inquire of the prophetess Huldah concerning the judgments the law threatened, all of it running parallel, they note, to the older narrative at 2 Kings 22:11-20. The witnesses do not divide. Wesley marks the freshness of the word to a man who had never heard it; Henry the holy fear it wrought and the inward rending it demands; Keil the dismay that would send the king seeking a prophetic word. Between them they show the difference between a king who sought God and a king who merely kept the forms: Josiah had purged the land, repaired the house, and gathered the offering, yet when the law itself was read to him he did not congratulate himself on his reforms but tore his robes in terror at how far the nation had fallen short. It is the mark of a heart truly tender that the word of God humbles even its friends — and that tenderness, the coming oracle will say, is the very thing that spares him.
